Cedar Park's Restaurant Boom Is Skipping Whitestone Boulevard

If you had to guess where Cedar Park's next wave of restaurants was landing, you'd probably say Whitestone Boulevard. It's the strip everyone already pictures when they think of eating out here, the corridor with the shopping centers and the drive time everybody already knows by heart. That guess would be wrong, and knowing why matters more than it sounds like it should.

The restaurants opening in Cedar Park through the rest of 2026 are clustering in two places that have nothing to do with Whitestone. One is a patch of ground on the Cedar Park-Leander line that didn't have a restaurant address six months ago. The other is a development taking shape behind H-E-B Center that isn't really about restaurants at all. Meanwhile, the corridor you already know is spending this fall under construction cones.

The corridor you already know is getting harder to drive through

Whitestone Boulevard has been the default answer to "where do you eat in Cedar Park" for years, and that's not changing overnight. But right now it's also the epicenter of the city's road work. Cedar Park and TxDOT have road improvements underway from New Hope Drive to Bagdad Road, plus a redesigned intersection near Whitestone Boulevard and 183A Toll, a combined project running $11.9 million for the roadway and $15.9 million for the intersection. New Hope Drive itself is being widened from four lanes to six as part of that same work, with the intersection targeted for completion this winter and the full road stretching into winter 2027. A separate state-led project is also underway a few miles north, adding frontage roads along 183A Toll between East Whitestone Boulevard and Avery Ranch Boulevard, a $139 million build that isn't expected to wrap until fall 2027.

None of that means Whitestone is going anywhere. It means if you already treat that corridor as your default, this fall is going to feel more like detours and lane shifts than a smooth drive to dinner. Which makes the timing of everything opening elsewhere even harder to ignore.

Two new pockets, and they're pulling in opposite directions

The clearest sign that Cedar Park's dining scene is reorganizing itself is the New Hope-Scottsdale Development, a patch of land straddling the Cedar Park-Leander border that didn't exist as a commercial address a year ago. Three known Austin-area restaurant names are landing there at once: Salt Traders Coastal Cooking, Day Maker Half Day Cafe, and Pinthouse Pizza. Construction on all three is slated to begin this September, with completion expected by June 2027.

Day Maker is notable because it's not a first-time concept rolling the dice. It's a second location from the same restaurant team behind Jack Allen's Kitchen and Salt Traders, following its original South Austin debut in late 2024. Pinthouse, meanwhile, is bringing something bigger than a standard restaurant footprint: a 13,640-square-foot restaurant and brewery building with a covered canopy and outdoor beer garden, a $7.43 million build that will be Pinthouse's sixth location alongside three in Austin, one in Round Rock, and one in San Antonio.

That's three known operators choosing to open on the same undeveloped stretch at the same time, rather than filling empty storefronts on an existing strip. That's not infill. That's a restaurant row being built from raw ground.

On the opposite side of the city, behind H-E-B Center on Avenue of the Stars, a very different kind of cluster is forming. CedarView is bringing a Cedar Park Convention Center, a Marriott hotel, and big-box anchors including Nebraska Furniture Mart and Scheels Sporting Goods, with Scheels reportedly beginning its hiring process in early 2026 for something in the range of 500 jobs. This isn't a food pocket. It's a hospitality and retail pocket, and it's happening at the same time, on the same side of the highway system, as the New Hope-Scottsdale build.

Here's how the two compare heading into fall 2026:

New Hope-Scottsdale (Cedar Park-Leander line) CedarView (behind H-E-B Center)
Salt Traders Coastal Cooking: construction begins this fall, complete by June 2027 Nebraska Furniture Mart: anchor tenant, build-out underway
Day Maker Half Day Cafe: second location, same fall-to-2027 timeline Scheels Sporting Goods: hiring underway, roughly 500 jobs
Pinthouse Pizza: $7.43 million restaurant and brewery, same window Marriott Hotel and Cedar Park Convention Center: site anchors

If you live closer to the 183A Toll and New Hope Drive side of the city, you're getting a restaurant row. If you're closer to H-E-B Center, you're getting a hotel and convention district. Same city, same year, two entirely different kinds of growth.

What's already open, not just coming soon

Not everything is still on paper. The Peached Tortilla's Backyard, a family-oriented outdoor expansion of its Cedar Park location with a playscape, Adirondack chairs, and picnic tables, opened February 17, 2026, with its own separate menu and a daily social hour where drinks start at $5.

PopStroke, the Tiger Woods-affiliated mini-golf and dining concept, filed for an April opening at 817 C-Bar Ranch Trail as a $5.8 million venture featuring two 18-hole courses, a full-service scratch kitchen, an ice cream parlor, three bars, and an outdoor beer garden. If that timeline held, it's already been open for months by now.

The restaurants aren't filling gaps in Cedar Park's existing map. They're drawing a new one.

Two more names are worth watching by name specifically. Conejos Tex-Mex Cantina, expanding from its original Leander location, is targeting an October or November 2026 opening in Cedar Park, with the same fajitas-and-enchiladas menu as the original. And J. Alexander's is aiming for a fall 2026 debut at 750 E. New Hope Drive, a $4.25 million build with construction that began in the spring, though no official opening date has been locked in as of the latest filing.

How the two sides of the city are actually connected

The two pockets aren't as isolated from each other as the map might suggest. A new 10-foot-wide concrete shared-use path is currently under construction connecting 183A Toll to Bell Park along Brushy Creek Road, with completion targeted for this fall, the same season the New Hope-Scottsdale restaurants break ground. It's a small infrastructure detail, but it means the path infrastructure and the restaurant infrastructure are landing in the same few months.

That path also feeds into the broader Brushy Creek Trail system, which already links Twin Lakes Park near the YMCA through Brushy Creek Sports Park to the 90-acre Brushy Creek Lake Park, with its lake, splash pad, and kayak launch, and continues on to Champion Park before crossing into Round Rock. None of that trail mileage runs directly past either new development yet, but the city's stated direction, extending connectivity toward Bell Boulevard and eventually Lakeline Park, suggests the walking and biking network is trying to catch up to where the restaurants are actually landing rather than where they used to be.

What this actually changes about your next few months

If you've been circling back to the same three or four spots on Whitestone out of habit, this fall is the moment that habit gets tested, not because those places are going anywhere, but because the newest options aren't going to be there. They're going to be on a stretch of the Cedar Park-Leander line that didn't have a restaurant address a year ago, or behind a hockey arena where a convention center and a furniture superstore are taking shape.

None of this requires you to do anything differently today. Salt Traders, Day Maker, and Pinthouse won't have doors to walk through until at least next summer. Scheels is still hiring. But the pattern is worth knowing now, because by the time all of it opens, the corridor you already know will look like the smaller half of the story, not the whole thing.
